questions.corrige_markdown:
**Astrogeology** is the study of the geology of the Moon, the planets and other bodies in the Solar System.

**(i) Planet (2 marks).** A planet is a large body which **orbits a star** (the Sun, for us), is massive enough for its own gravity to make it **nearly spherical**, and has **cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit** of other debris. It does not make its own light but shines by **reflected sunlight**. There are eight planets in the Solar System: the rocky terrestrial planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) and the giant planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune).

**(ii) Asteroids (2 marks).** Asteroids are **small rocky or metallic bodies** (from a few metres to hundreds of kilometres across) which **orbit the Sun**, most of them in the **asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter**. They are left over from the formation of the Solar System, because the gravity of Jupiter prevented them from joining into a planet. They are the source of most meteorites.

**(iii) Solar system (2 marks).** The Solar System is the **Sun and all the bodies that are held by its gravity and orbit it**: the eight planets and their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and meteoroids, and dust and gas. It formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a rotating cloud of gas and dust (the solar nebula) in the Milky Way galaxy, and it contains more than 99 per cent of its mass in the Sun.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Outline five differences between the Oceanic and the Continental lithospheres.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **lithosphere** is the rigid outer layer of the Earth (crust and the uppermost, rigid part of the mantle) which forms the plates. Five differences between the oceanic and the continental lithosphere are given (the values are typical, approximate ones).

| Feature | Oceanic lithosphere | Continental lithosphere |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Thickness | Thin: crust about 5 to 10 km, whole lithosphere about 50 to 100 km (thickening with age) | Thick: crust about 30 to 70 km (up to 70 km under mountains), whole lithosphere about 100 to 200 km |
| 2. Composition of the crust | **Basaltic and gabbroic (mafic)**, rich in silicon, magnesium and iron (**sima**), with a thin cover of sediment | **Granitic to andesitic (felsic)** rich in silicon and aluminium (**sial**), plus sedimentary and metamorphic rocks |
| 3. Density | Higher: about 2.9 to 3.0 $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ | Lower: about 2.7 $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ |
| 4. Age | **Young**: nowhere older than about 180 to 200 million years, because it is made at ridges and destroyed at trenches | **Old**: parts are up to about 4 billion years old |
| 5. Behaviour at plate boundaries | Dense, so it **sinks (subducts)** below continental or older oceanic lithosphere | Light and buoyant, so it **does not subduct** and is preserved, and it is crumpled in collisions |
| 6. Structure and relief | Layered (sediment, pillow lavas, sheeted dykes, gabbro); forms ocean floor about 4 to 5 km below sea level | Complex and variable; forms the continents, mostly above sea level |

(Any five correct differences score full marks.)
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) State the possible causes of earthquakes.

(4 marks)

(ii) Give the properties of transverse waves.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Possible causes of earthquakes (4 marks).** An earthquake is a sudden release of energy in the Earth which produces seismic waves.

1. **Tectonic movements (the main cause).** Plates move slowly and the rocks at their edges are strained until the stress is larger than the strength of the rock, and then the rocks **break and slip along a fault** (the **elastic rebound** theory). This accounts for most earthquakes, at plate boundaries (subduction zones, transform faults, ridges and collision zones).
2. **Volcanic activity.** The movement of magma, the explosion of a volcano, or the collapse of a magma chamber produce shocks (mostly of small magnitude), which can also be a warning of an eruption.
3. **Human activities (induced earthquakes).** Filling of large reservoirs behind dams, deep mining and the collapse of mine roofs, underground explosions and nuclear tests, injection of fluid into the ground.
4. **Other causes.** Landslides, the collapse of the roofs of caves (limestone areas), **isostatic readjustment** after the melting of ice, and the meteorite impacts.

**(ii) Properties of transverse (S) waves (10 marks).** Transverse waves are also called **secondary, shear or S waves**. They are one of the two types of **body waves** (with P waves).

1. The **particles of rock vibrate at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction of travel** of the wave (a transverse or shear motion, as in a shaken rope), producing a **shearing** of the rock without a change of its volume.
2. They **travel only through solids**, because a liquid has **no rigidity** (shear strength). They **cannot pass through the liquid outer core**, which leaves an **S-wave shadow zone** on the side of the Earth opposite to the focus (from about 103° to 180° from the epicentre). This is the proof that the outer core is liquid.
3. They are **slower than P waves** (about 60 per cent of their speed) and **arrive second** on a seismogram. Their speed depends on the rigidity $\mu$ and the density $\rho$: $v_S = \sqrt{\mu/\rho}$. Typical speed is about 3.5 to 4.5 $\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ in the crust and upper mantle, and a little more in the lower mantle.
4. The **time interval between the arrival of the P and S waves** (the S-P interval) is used to find the **distance of the epicentre** from the station, and three stations give its position (triangulation).
5. They have a **larger amplitude** than P waves and are **more destructive** (they shake the ground from side to side and up and down), but they have a lower frequency and they are **absorbed** more.
6. They can be **polarised** into SV (vertical) and SH (horizontal) components, and they are **reflected, refracted and converted** at boundaries such as the Mohorovicic discontinuity (Moho) and the core-mantle boundary at about 2900 km. They show a **sudden change of velocity** at these boundaries, which is evidence for the layered structure of the Earth's interior.
7. They cause the **ground to move sideways**, which can shear foundations of buildings and structures.
